exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: Report an experiment with its hypothesis, sample, observations, and next decision.
exampleAnswers.Working context: In this fictional usability exercise, twelve participants tried two versions of a document index. The numbers illustrate reporting structure and are not a statistically validated product claim.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Version: A · file list · Task completed: 4 · Participants: 6 · Observed completion: 67% rounded
Version: B · owned index · Task completed: 5 · Participants: 6 · Observed completion: 83% rounded
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Hypothesis and method: An index with purpose and owner labels may help a new collaborator find the correct handover document. Each participant attempted the same lookup task using one assigned version.
What we observed: Five of six participants completed the task with the owned index, compared with four of six using the file list. The small sample and one-task design limit the conclusions.
Next decision: Keep the clearer labels for a broader trial and test with more varied tasks. Do not describe the difference as statistically significant or as proof of a general productivity gain.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: deck layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching landscape presentation PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
